motive: Ill-treatment by the appellant for not arranging money from her mother
key_evidence_accepted: The medical expert admitted that the rope found on the spot could have been used for suicidal hanging and that in case of homicidal strangulation, bodily resistance would be reflected. However, there were no marks on the body suggesting violence or struggle, and the medical expert did not rule out the possibility of suicidal death.
witness_credibility: The court disbelieved the evidence of PW-1, stating it was full of improvements and omissions. The court also found the uncorroborated evidence of PW-3 (the mother of the deceased) unreliable as it showed cordial relations between the accused and deceased.
trial_duration: Dates of offence: 23rd March 2003; Trial judgment: 1st October 2008; High Court decision: Not stated; Supreme Court decision: March 02, 2021
legal_representation: Counsel for the accused: S. Mahendran, Aaditya A. Pande, Geo Joseph; Counsel for the State: Sachin Patil
investigation_status: FIR registered, charge sheet filed, trial completed
appeal_history: Trial court: Convicted under s.302 and sentenced to imprisonment for life; High Court: Upheld the order; Supreme Court: Appeal allowed, conviction and sentence set aside, appellant acquitted
prosecution_argument: The prosecution argued that the appellant was addicted to liquor and abused his wife, forcing her to get money from her mother. They claimed the deceased committed suicide by hanging, but the trial court and High Court convicted the appellant under Section 302 IPC for homicidal death.
defence_argument: The defence argued that the prosecution failed to prove the death was homicidal, as the medical expert admitted the possibility of suicidal hanging. The prosecution's motive-based evidence was uncorroborated and lacked credibility, failing to establish a chain of circumstances beyond reasonable doubt.
legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the principle that in cases of circumstantial evidence, the prosecution must prove the guilt beyond reasonable doubt, and if two views are possible, the benefit shall always go to the accused.
precedent_relied_upon: Eswarappa alias Doopada Eswarappa v. State of Karnataka (2019) 16 SCC 269; Subramaniam v. State of Tamil Nadu and Another (2009) 14 SCC 415; Gargi v. State of Haryana (2019) 9 SCC 738; Anwar Ali and Another v. State of Himachal Pradesh (2020) 10 SCC 166; Sharad Birdhichand Sarda v. State of Maharashtra (1984) 4 SCC 116
